meta.summary: A concise introduction to spaced repetition: forgetting curves, SM-2 style scheduling, retrieval practice, common mistakes, and how to start with atomic cards.
learningObjectives: Explain the forgetting curve and why spacing helps
Describe how SM-2 adjusts interval and ease from ratings
Identify card design mistakes that break SRS
Apply spaced review to a domain beyond language learning

transcript.text: Welcome. Today we are going to unpack spaced repetition—the idea that reviewing material at expanding intervals makes memories stick far better than cramming.

First, a quick prerequisite: memory is not a single store. Psychologists distinguish sensory memory, working memory, and long-term memory. Spaced repetition mainly trains the path into long-term memory.

The forgetting curve, popularized by Ebbinghaus in the late nineteenth century, shows that recall drops quickly after learning unless we reinforce it. The good news: each successful recall flattens that curve.
Definition: spaced repetition is a scheduling technique that presents an item for review just as you are about to forget it—often using an algorithm such as SM-2.
SM-2, originally from SuperMemo, tracks an ease factor and an interval. After you rate a card Again, Hard, Good, or Easy, the algorithm adjusts when you will see it next.
Core mechanism: retrieval practice. The act of recalling, not re-reading, strengthens the memory trace. Spacing adds difficulty in a productive way—desirable difficulty.

Example: imagine learning the Spanish word for apple. Day zero you learn it. Day one you recall it. Three days later you recall again. Then a week, then a month. Failures reset or shorten the interval.
A common mistake is making cards too broad. If a card asks for an entire essay, grading becomes noisy and the schedule cannot target the weak part. Prefer atomic facts or clear prompts.
Another mistake: passive highlighting without retrieval. Highlighting feels productive but does little unless you later force yourself to recall from cues.
Applications go beyond language decks. Engineers use spaced review for APIs and incident playbooks. Medical students use it for anatomy. Musicians space practice of difficult passages.

Argument: massed practice can produce short-term performance gains that fool you into thinking you have mastered the material. Spaced practice often looks worse in the moment but wins on delayed tests.
How to start: pick a tool—Anki, a simple JSON store like Learnyt, or paper flashcards. Capture one clear question and answer per card. Review daily, even for ten minutes.
When rating, be honest. If you barely recalled with hints, choose Hard or Again. Inflating Good ratings produces a pile of overdue cards later.

Takeaway one: memory is a skill of scheduling as much as of studying. Takeaway two: retrieval plus spacing beats rereading. Takeaway three: keep cards small and source-linked so you can jump back to context.
If you remember only one phrase from this talk, let it be desirable difficulty: the slight struggle of recalling at the right time is the feature, not the bug.
Thanks for watching. Try saving a few highlights from a real lecture into spaced repetition and rate them honestly for a week—you will feel the difference.
